At idle, the air hugs one wall and the other half of the diffuser flows backwards

Steady CFD of the inlet diffuser at 40,000 rpm, 7.42 g/s per inlet. Only 28 % of the bore's dynamic pressure comes back as static pressure; a good straight diffuser returns 60–70 %.

Ansys Fluent 2026 R1, mid-plane velocity vectors (m/s). Select the image to enlarge it.

Why it stalls

The walls open faster than the slow air near them can follow the rising pressure, and the entry step removes the attached wall layer before the taper even starts.

Wall angle, wide plane
16.5°

About twice the 8–10° a straight diffuser of this length (L/W₁ = 9.9) can follow without stalling. The thin plane opens at only 2°.

Sudden step, Ø6 → 7 × 7 mm
18 %

Of the bore's dynamic pressure, about 6 kPa, lost at once (Borda–Carnot), and the taper starts with separated flow.

Plate orientation
Height, not width

The five plates are stacked through the 9.4 mm height, so they can't even out a side-to-side imbalance.

The equivalent cone angle is only 8.4°, inside the usual limit. It hides the problem because it spreads the opening around a round cone, while here all of it happens on two walls.

Design options

Each fix changes one thing; the combinations follow. Only today's numbers come from CFD. The Cp values for the fixes are estimates from straight-diffuser data (Reneau et al. 1967), and the supply pressure each one needs is computed from its Cp.

Fix 1: longer taper

estimate

What changes. The taper is 127 mm long instead of 69 mm. The start and the 27 mm exit stay the same.

Result. The walls open at only 9 degrees, so the air can stay on both walls. Nothing is added inside.

The catch. The part gets 58 mm longer: only possible if the test stand has the room.

Fix 2: smooth entry

estimate

What changes. The 6 mm bore blends smoothly into the 7 mm square instead of jumping.

Result. Removes the jump loss and gives the air a clean start.

The catch. The walls still open at 16.5 degrees, so the side stall stays. It helps, but it does not fix it alone.

Fix 3: two splitter vanes

estimate

What changes. Two thin upright vanes inside the taper, from x = 15 to 62 mm. The outside stays as today.

Result. The vanes split the wide angle into three channels inside the 8-10 degree guide, so the air spreads over the full width.

The catch. The vanes must point exactly along the flow. The entry step stays.

Evidence from the CFD

The problem lives in the wide plane. In the thin plane the jet stays centred. Select an image to enlarge it.

How far to trust it

The one-sided stall matches decades of diffuser experiments for this angle and length, so the pattern is solid. The exact numbers are first estimates until the open checks are done.

  • Mass balanceIn and out agree within 0.11 %.
    Done
  • ResidualsFlat after about 1,300 iterations, but continuity stays near 1e-2 (usual target 1e-3): a sign of unsteady separation.
    Explained
  • Mesh-independence studyOne mesh so far; the numbers can still move.
    Not started
  • y+ on the final meshTargeted y+ = 1 for SST; not yet checked on the walls.
    Not checked
  • Short transient runA steady solver picks one wall; on the rig the stall may switch sides.
    Not started
  • Stand boundary conditionsOutlet 1 atm and 300 K are assumptions until the stand data arrives.
    Assumed
  • Exit uniformity indexThe first number to add for comparing the fixes.
    Not computed
  • 1D model against the CFDAt the CFD's Cp the 1D model needs 23.7 kPa of supply pressure; Fluent needed 24 kPa (-1.5 %).
    Done

How the numbers are computed

Every number on this page is computed in Python from the raw Fluent values in data/fluent_baseline.json and the geometry in data/options.json. Air: γ = 1.4, R = 287 J/(kg·K), T₀ = 300 K, outlet at 1 atm.

What happens next

First make the baseline solid, then test the recommended fix, then the higher engine speeds.

  1. 1
    Make the baseline solidMesh-independence study and a y+ check on the final mesh.
  2. 2
    Run a short transientSee whether the stall stays on one wall or switches, as it may on the rig.
  3. 3
    Test vanes + smooth entrySame envelope, same mesh settings. Compare supply pressure, loss, Cp, exit uniformity and wall shear.
  4. 4
    Go to higher rpmRepeat at the higher mass flows and check the Ø6 bore stays below Mach 1.
Sources for the design guidance:
  • Kline, Abbott and Fox (1959), Optimum design of straight-walled diffusers.
  • Reneau, Johnston and Kline (1967), Performance and design of straight, two-dimensional diffusers.
  • Moore and Kline (1958), Effects of vanes in wide-angle diffusers, NACA TN-4080.
  • Dixon and Hall (2014), Fluid Mechanics and Thermodynamics of Turbomachinery, ch. 7.
